name: Gene-editing therapies
summary: Therapies alter a patient’s DNA in collected cells or directly in the body to address selected disease mechanisms.
useCase: A specialist centre collects a patient’s stem cells, edits them, and reinfuses them after conditioning for an approved inherited blood disorder.
whyNow: The first approved CRISPR therapy has moved from regulatory breakthrough into commercial delivery. The remaining challenge is expanding access safely and proving in-body editing across more diseases.

mainstream.scope: Established treatment option at specialist centres for selected severe inherited diseases; in-vivo indications only after successful trials and approval.
mainstream.rationale: Approved ex-vivo treatment and rising launch revenue establish a commercial base. Conditioning, specialised capacity, reimbursement and long-term follow-up make broad access gradual. Many proposed in-vivo indications can slip past 2035.

metric.name: Casgevy annual net product revenue
metric.scope: Vertex-recognised global Casgevy revenue; launch-stage company proxy
metric.limitations: Revenue for one therapy is not the gene-editing market or number of successfully treated patients. The large change begins from an initial launch year; price, timing and access affect revenue.
metric.futureNote: No defensible like-for-like external forecast is available for this KPI. The forward maturity path is a separately labelled analyst scenario, not a numerical adoption forecast.

milestones.text: No approved US CRISPR therapy existed in the historical baseline; no revenue measure is assigned.
No comparable commercial revenue observation is included for 2022.
FDA approved Casgevy for sickle cell disease in December, the first FDA-approved CRISPR/Cas9 treatment.
FDA added transfusion-dependent beta thalassemia in January; Casgevy generated $10 million during its first full launch year.
Casgevy net product revenue reached $115.8 million.
Vertex announced expanded US approval of Casgevy in July for specified indications in patients ages two and older. Long-term safety follow-up remains necessary.

tailwinds: A single intervention can address a defined genetic cause
Editing tools and delivery systems can support multiple programmes
Manufacturing and treatment-centre capacity can be reused
bottlenecks: Conditioning and treatment burden for current ex-vivo approaches
Off-target effects, durability and long-term follow-up
High upfront cost and difficult reimbursement logistics
watchMetrics: Patients infused rather than treatment centres announced
Serious adverse events and durability by indication
Time from referral to treatment and reimbursement completion
